questions.q: What are the three governance pillars this lesson identifies for an MDM program?
options: Domain ownership, standards and rules, and stewardship workflow
Server uptime, network latency, and disk capacity
Marketing budget, sales quota, and headcount
Software license cost, vendor support tier, and renewal date
questions.explain: The lesson names domain ownership, written standards/rules, and a defined stewardship workflow as the three pillars that keep an MDM program from drifting back into chaos.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the relationship between an MDM data steward and the general data steward role from Data Governance Foundations?
options: They are entirely unrelated roles with no connection
The MDM data steward replaces the data steward role and makes it obsolete
An MDM data steward is a data steward whose scope is specifically master data matching and merging — the role extends, not replaces, the earlier one
MDM data stewards have no accountability for data quality at all
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that MDM roles extend the data owner/steward roles already introduced in Data Governance Foundations rather than creating something unrelated.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what happens to an MDM program that has no written governance?
options: It automatically improves in quality over time with no intervention
Matching rules drift, ownership of new fields goes undefined, and the 'single source of truth' can quietly fork again
Nothing changes — governance has no measurable effect
It becomes immune to future data quality issues
questions.explain: The lesson opens by warning that an MDM program without governance doesn't stay fixed — rules drift and the single trusted view can re-fragment within a year.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a usable written MDM policy cover, at minimum?
options: Only the names of the software vendors involved
Which domains are in scope, who owns each one, the match rules and confidence thresholds, survivorship rules, and who can approve changes
A list of every employee's salary
Nothing — MDM policies are described as unnecessary overhead
questions.explain: The lesson lists domain scope, ownership, match rules/thresholds, survivorship rules, and change-approval authority as the minimum content of a usable MDM policy.

questions.q: What does this lesson say Chapter 2 will cover, now that Chapter 1 has closed?
options: A return to governance frameworks covered in Data Governance Foundations
The hands-on mechanics of matching records, deduplication, golden records, survivorship rules, and steward review
A detailed history of MDM software vendors
Reference data governance exclusively
questions.explain: The lesson closes Chapter 1 by previewing Chapter 2 as the hands-on matching-and-consolidation chapter, starting with data matching concepts.
